did_you_know.text: This verse opens Judah’s land allotment — the southern border reaches the Negev and desert, a semi‑arid zone where water and grazing were crucial.
The “Sea of Salt” here is the Dead Sea — a key landmark for southern boundaries.
The Ascent of Scorpions (Ma'aleh Akrabbim) is named as a southern route; the name evokes a steep, hazardous pass in antiquity.
The Brook of Egypt (Nahal Mizrayim) marks the southwestern border; it is often identified with Wadi el‑Arish in geographical studies.
“The Great Sea” refers to the Mediterranean — Judah’s western border reached the coastal plain.
The verse names springs such as Ein Shemesh and Ein Rogel, which served as boundary markers and vital water sources for the hill country around Jerusalem.
The Valley of Ben‑Hinnom is mentioned — this same valley later becomes associated in tradition with “Gehenna,” carrying religious connotations in later texts.
Caleb is given Kiriath‑arba (Hebron) — an example of a personal allotment within the tribal land distribution.
The three sons of Anak (Sheshai, Ahiman, Talmai) are named; in the biblical tradition the Anakim are portrayed as a formidable clan, often associated with great stature.
Debir also appears under its older name Kiriath‑Sepher — two names for the same site that recur in the conquest and inheritance narratives.
Caleb’s promise to give his daughter to whoever captures the city shows a custom where military success could be rewarded with marriage ties.
Othniel son of Kenaz captured the town and married Achsah — the name Othniel also appears later as one of Israel’s judges.
Achsah asks for a blessing and specifically requests springs of water — upper and lower springs; the appeal highlights how vital water sources were in the Negev.
The verse closes by stating this is Judah’s inheritance — such concluding formulas fix the lists of towns and territory in Joshua.
Ziklag is listed here — in a later narrative (Samuel) David uses Ziklag as a temporary refuge, so its mention connects to later stories.
The formula “all the cities twenty‑nine and their villages” repeats in these lists — it indicates that not just towns but their surrounding rural holdings were part of the allotment.
The term “Shephelah” denotes the lowland plain between the coastal strip and the Judean hills — an agriculturally important zone in antiquity.
The mention of Ashdod, Gaza and the Brook of Egypt shows Judah’s western claims touched Philistine cities and reached the Egyptian frontier.
Ein Gedi is an oasis on the Dead Sea shore; in other biblical passages David is said to have taken refuge in this area.
The Jebusites, inhabitants of Jerusalem, were not driven out by Judah — the biblical tradition records that Jerusalem was conquered later by David.
